Records show partner Jay Lefkowitz led the defense and negotiated the 2008 non-prosecution agreement with US Attorney Alexander Acosta, who had been a Kirkland associate in the firm's Washington office from 1995 to 1997 [Finding #3108]. According to LittleSis and public records, several Kirkland alumni held senior Department of Justice and White House positions during the first Trump administration, including Attorney General William Barr, Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen, Criminal Division head Brian Benczkowski, and White House Counsel Pat Cipollone [Finding #3091][Finding #3159]. According to contemporaneous news reporting, in April 2025 the firm agreed to provide $125 million in pro bono legal services for Trump-administration-approved causes as part of a broader multi-firm arrangement that followed a threatened executive order [Finding #3099][Finding #3158].

Court records show partner Mark Filip, a former Deputy Attorney General, led Kirkland's corporate criminal defense work on BP Deepwater Horizon ($4.525 billion criminal resolution, 2012), Volkswagen Dieselgate ($2.8 billion criminal penalty, 2017), and the Boeing 737 MAX deferred prosecution agreement ($2.5 billion, 2021) [Finding #3109][Finding #3154][Finding #3081]. Review of the filings found no evidence that Kirkland serves as primary outside counsel to Deutsche Bank, JPMorgan Chase, or Blackstone; according to that review, earlier-noted SEC EDGAR co-appearances were structural artifacts of Kirkland representing issuers while those banks served as underwriters [Finding #3170][Finding #3178].

sections.title: The Epstein Defense and NPA Negotiation
sections.content:
Records show Kirkland & Ellis represented Jeffrey Epstein in the 2007–2008 Florida federal matter, with partner Jay Lefkowitz as lead attorney [Finding #692][Finding #3100]. The defense team operated from the firm's New York office at 159 East 53rd Street and its DC office at 655 15th Street NW; a third named attorney, Michael D. Shumsky, appeared pro hac vice in the later SDFL CVRA proceedings [Finding #3071]. In a November 8, 2007 letter to prosecutors, Lefkowitz wrote that "Mr. Epstein is complying fully with the Non Prosecution Agreement and that he has every intention of continuing to honor its terms in good faith" and argued that Epstein's agents were not precluded from contacting potential witnesses — a claim prosecutors disputed, and which Lefkowitz only withdrew after SDFL objected [Finding #3080][EFTA00013698].

Kirkland's 17-page submission to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General argued that Epstein was "a successful businessman and noted philanthropist with no prior criminal record" whose conduct "falls within heartland of historic state police powers" [Finding #3072][EFTA00013811]. The submission sought to end federal involvement, argued the victims had lied about their ages, contested that any interstate facility was used for inducement, and challenged the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section's review as non-independent [Finding #3072]. A separate 10-page rebuttal of a May 2008 FAUSA letter recorded that prosecutors had threatened a 53-page indictment covering 40 minors with a 188-month guideline range, and alleged that the AUSA proposed an attorney representative who was her live-in boyfriend's former law school classmate [Finding #3079][EFTA00013801].

Both sides of the negotiation had institutional overlap with Kirkland. According to employment records, Alexander Acosta — the US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida — had been a Kirkland associate in the DC office from 1995 to 1997, the same office where Lefkowitz later worked [Finding #3108]. A 2018 Power Line article forwarded within the Epstein network stated that "Acosta reportedly worked out the terms of his surrender with Lefkowitz, a former colleague, at a meeting in a location far away from the prosecutor's office" [Finding #3076]. Ken Starr, a Kirkland partner and former Independent Counsel, lobbied Deputy Attorney General Mark Filip in a June 19, 2008 letter [Finding #3090][EFTA00013989]. In a December 9, 2018 defense memorandum later sent to Kathryn Ruemmler, Epstein described Filip as "with the exception of the Attorney General himself" the highest DOJ official to have reviewed and approved the NPA [Finding #3075][EFTA02612560].

Billing records show total Kirkland fees of $3,011,064 through September 30, 2009: $2,319,336 for the JEE defense through December 31, 2008, $100,000 for the FTC/DB Zwirn matter, and $591,728 in further billings that included $178,165 on the DOJ investigation, $173,965 on Jane Doe 101 litigation, and $10,247 on a Molyneux/Juan Pablo dispute [Finding #3061][Finding #3089][EFTA02413703]. Kirkland partner Scott D. Price served as second billing attorney alongside Lefkowitz, with rates between $1,045 and $1,095 per hour [Finding #3062]. Physical defense materials — including Kirkland invoices, the retention agreement, and a Kirkland April 8, 2008 letter to the DOJ alleging prosecutorial misconduct — were later catalogued in the GRM Master Filing Index [Finding #3077][Finding #3107]. Epstein visited Kirkland's offices for a three-hour meeting on March 2, 2010, with meetings scheduled the same day with Peter Mandelson and Jes Staley [Finding #3069][EFTA02428729]. In April 2012, Epstein directed a referral to Kirkland, writing "tell frank the law firm is called kirkland, and ellis, jay lefokowitz is head of litigation" [Finding #3089]. Five months before his death, Epstein emailed Ruemmler, "why isnt kirkland and ellis defending this npa in front of marra, it is their agreement that i followed? pled, registered and paid money. do they have an obligation to defend it?" [Finding #3065][Finding #3092][EFTA02633736]. In a February 23, 2019 email, criminal-defense attorney David Schoen wrote that "lefkowitz and every other lawyer involved in your deal ought to understand in no uncertain terms that if you end up, G-d forbid, having a problem from this, they face major exposure" [Finding #3067][EFTA02634297].

sections.title: DOJ and White House Alumni
sections.content:
Multiple Kirkland & Ellis alumni have moved between the firm and senior federal government positions. According to LittleSis, the database maps 131 relationships around the firm, and public records identify at least twenty-two confirmed Kirkland alumni who held senior government positions across the Trump, Obama, and Biden administrations [Finding #3087][Finding #3086].

During the first Trump administration, Attorney General William Barr served as Kirkland Of Counsel from 2009 and as a consultant in 2011 on the BP matter before returning as Of Counsel from 2017 to 2018 [Finding #3086][Finding #3057]. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen was a longtime Kirkland partner whose corporate clients had included Raytheon, General Motors, and the Chamber of Commerce [Finding #3091]. Brian Benczkowski, who ran the Criminal Division overseeing corporate prosecutions, had been a Kirkland partner who represented Alfa Bank in March 2017 in the investigation of alleged communications with the Trump Organization [Finding #3102]. Review of the records shows Benczkowski received an ethics waiver to participate in the Goldman Sachs 1MDB case despite Kirkland having represented Goldman [Finding #3088]. Jeffrey Clark was a Kirkland partner from 1996 to 2018 [Finding #3091]. White House Counsel Pat Cipollone and deputies Patrick Philbin and John Eisenberg were all former Kirkland partners [Finding #3093]. Public records show at least twelve former Kirkland lawyers in senior DOJ or White House positions during that administration [Finding #3091][Finding #3159].

Alumni have also held senior Democratic-administration posts. Review of the records shows Neil Eggleston served as Obama's White House Counsel (2014–2017) between stints as a Kirkland partner, and Ali Zaidi became Biden's National Climate Advisor (2022–2025) after serving as a Kirkland partner representing fossil-fuel clients including Mission Coal, Murray Energy, and Blackstone [Finding #3113]. Review of the records further shows Richard Cordray, the first Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, was Kirkland Of Counsel, and Susan Davies, a Kirkland partner who represented Facebook in antitrust, was considered for Biden's AAG for Antitrust [Finding #3113].

Beyond the DOJ, John Bolton served as National Security Advisor (2018–2019) after a decade as Kirkland Of Counsel, Alex Azar served as HHS Secretary (2018–2021) after working as a Kirkland associate, and Christopher Landau was a Kirkland partner for 25 years before serving as Ambassador to Mexico [Finding #3094]. Brett Kavanaugh was a Kirkland partner (1997–1998 and 1999–2001) before his appointment to the D.C. Circuit and subsequent elevation to the Supreme Court [Finding #3095][Finding #3057]. According to Senate confirmation records, Steven Bradbury, a Kirkland litigation partner from 1993 to 2004 who led the Office of Legal Counsel during the torture-memos era, was confirmed as Deputy Secretary of Transportation in March 2025, and John Eisenberg was confirmed as AAG for the National Security Division in June 2025 [Finding #3111][Finding #3160]. Records show that across the periods 2008–2012, 2015–2021, 2018–2020, and 2025, Kirkland alumni held senior government posts concurrent with the firm's $125 million pro bono commitment to the second Trump administration [Finding #3161][Finding #3099].

sections.title: Corporate Criminal Defense and the Filip Memo
sections.content:
Mark Filip is the principal Kirkland partner associated with the firm's corporate criminal defense practice. Review of the records shows that as Deputy Attorney General, Filip authored the "Filip Memorandum" on August 28, 2008, which revised DOJ guidelines for corporate prosecutions to protect attorney-client privilege during investigations [Finding #3156]. Records show he joined Kirkland in May 2009 and over the following fifteen years defended corporations under the framework he had written [Finding #3156]. Records show his former chief of staff, Brian Benczkowski, co-counseled Kirkland corporate matters before serving as AAG for the Criminal Division from 2018 to 2020 and then returning to the firm [Finding #3088][Finding #3166].

Court records show that in the BP Deepwater Horizon matter, Kirkland (led by Filip) and Gibson Dunn represented BP Exploration and Production, which pleaded guilty in 2012 to 14 felony counts — 11 manslaughter counts, one felony Clean Water Act count, one obstruction of Congress count, and one Migratory Bird Treaty Act count — in a $4.525 billion criminal resolution [Finding #3084][Finding #3154]. According to court records, all four individual BP executives charged either had charges dropped (rig supervisors Robert Kaluza and Donald Vidrine saw their 11 manslaughter counts each dismissed in December 2015), pleaded to misdemeanors with probation, or were acquitted; none received prison time [Finding #3155]. According to Bloomberg reporting from September 23, 2015 and subsequent court records, VW hired Kirkland for the Dieselgate emissions-scandal defense, ultimately pleaded guilty, paid a $2.8 billion criminal penalty, and accepted three-year probation with an independent compliance monitor [Finding #3085]. According to court records in Case 4:21-cr-00005 (NDTX, filed January 7, 2021), Filip signed the Boeing 737 MAX deferred prosecution agreement on behalf of Boeing; terms totalled $2.5 billion, comprising a $243.6 million criminal penalty, a $500 million victim fund, and $1.77 billion in airline-customer compensation, after a conspiracy-to-defraud charge tied to 346 deaths in two crashes [Finding #3081][Finding #3157]. Records indicate Columbia Law Professor John Coffee described the DPA as "one of the worst deferred prosecution agreements I have seen," and the resolution did not include a compliance monitor [Finding #3081][Finding #3157].

According to court and firm records, Erin Nealy Cox — the US Attorney for the Northern District of Texas who oversaw the Boeing case — resigned effective January 9, 2021 (the same day the DPA was filed in her district) and joined Kirkland as a partner in Dallas on June 23, 2021 [Finding #3082]. Records show crash victims' families initially alleged impropriety but withdrew the claims in January 2022 [Finding #3082]. Court records indicate Boeing later breached the DPA in 2024, and the DOJ dropped the prosecution in May 2025 in favor of a non-prosecution agreement [Finding #3081][Finding #3157]. According to The American Prospect, cross-comparison of the 2008 Epstein NPA and the 2021 Boeing DPA — both Kirkland-led negotiations resulting in no federal trial and limited victim consultation — is discussed in the outlet's piece "Blowing the Door Off Boeing's Epstein Deal" [Finding #3104][Finding #3115].

sections.title: Network Position and Client Relationships
sections.content:
Analysis of the documented relationships indicates Kirkland & Ellis is among the more heavily connected institutional entities in the network, behind Jeffrey Epstein and William Barr, and comparable in its bridging position to Leon Black [Finding #3179]. The analysis indicates the firm functions as a structural bridge: most of the entities it connects to are not otherwise linked to one another [Finding #3179]. According to the records, three variant spellings of the firm's name ("Kirkland & Ellis", "Kirkland and Ellis", "Kirkland Ellis") resolve to a single entity [Finding #3470][Finding #5439].

A later review corrected the firm's financial-sector client map. Analysis of thousands of SEC EDGAR co-appearances with Deutsche Bank (7,048 filings), JPMorgan Chase (6,593), and Blackstone (2,346) had earlier inferred client relationships from those filings [Finding #3055]. Review of the filings — including Deutsche Bank's 20-F, JPMorgan's 10-K, and Blackstone's 10-K — found no evidence that Kirkland serves as primary outside counsel to any of the three: each contained zero Kirkland references, Blackstone's primary outside counsel is Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, and the co-appearances are artifacts of Kirkland representing issuers and private-equity sponsors while those banks served as underwriters, indenture trustees, or financial advisors in the same transactions [Finding #3170][Finding #3178][Finding #3177]. Review of the records shows Kirkland does have documented Deutsche Bank engagements in specific matters, including the CFTC precious-metals spoofing settlement ($30 million), shareholder litigation following the forex investigation, and the MidOcean Partners $1.6 billion spin-off [Finding #3170].

Kirkland's confirmed institutional-client relationships, by contrast, are documented via firm press releases and securities filings. The firm represents Apollo Global Management on fund-level portfolio acquisitions, including Apollo funds' strategic investment in T.D. Williamson (June 2025) and the Smart & Final Stores tender offer (May 2019) [Finding #3165][Finding #3169]. It served as counsel to Caesars Entertainment Operating Company — an Apollo-controlled Caesars subsidiary — in its Chapter 11 bankruptcy filed in January 2015, and as counsel to Energy Future Holdings Corp in the Chapter 11 tied to the Apollo/KKR/TPG LBO of TXU [Finding #3163][Finding #3164]. Kirkland is ongoing outside counsel to Cerberus Capital Management on multiple acquisitions, including Staples' European business (December 2016), SubCom (September 2018), and the Cerberus-Koch acquisition of PQ Corporation (March 2021) [Finding #3167]. Review of the records indicates Kirkland represented Goldman Sachs in the 1MDB investigation during the period when alumni Barr and Benczkowski held senior DOJ positions [Finding #3166]. According to a separate August 2016 Law360 article forwarded to Epstein by Nicholas Ribis, Kirkland appeared as Apollo counsel in the Caesars Entertainment bankruptcy litigation alongside Jones Day [Finding #3074][EFTA02452464].

The Kirkland & Ellis Foundation (EIN 36-3160355, Chicago IL) is a separate 501(c)(3) entity from the law firm, with continuous 990 filings since 2006; revenue peaked at $25.5 million in 2016 and settled to $8.6 million by 2023, with no grants documented to Epstein-connected entities [Finding #3053][990:363160355]. Kirkland has 20 LDA lobbying registrations since 1999 under registrant ID 21745, with reported client income including CBOT ($400,000 in 1999), Verizon ($40,000), and General Motors ($40,000) [Finding #3054][Finding #3105]. The firm's only known FARA registration is No. 4558 (August 22, 1991 – May 3, 1995) for Goodman Holdings and Anglo Irish Beef Processors, and has no documented connection to the investigation's core subjects [Finding #3098][Finding #3052][FARA:4558]. Kirkland is registered as a foreign LLP in DC (file 210204, effective July 2, 2003; principal address 300 North LaSalle, Chicago IL 60654) [Finding #3051][REG:DC:210204]. According to LittleSis entity 28533, the database maps 50 documented relationships for the firm, including a business relationship with Epstein (LittleSis relationship 2021528) and a consultancy relationship with former Israeli Ambassador Michael Oren [Finding #3110][Finding #3112]. According to Federalist Society records, alumni including Kavanaugh, Starr, Robert Bork, Bolton, Eisenberg, Viet Dinh, and Bradbury are members or speakers, and Kirkland has sponsored the society's annual dinner [Finding #3103]. Records show that in 2022, former Solicitor General Paul Clement left Kirkland after the firm announced it would no longer handle Second Amendment litigation [Finding #3103].

sections.title: Starr, Lefkowitz, and Post-NPA Contacts
sections.content:
Evidence in the DOJ corpus documents continued contact between several Kirkland partners and Epstein well beyond the 2008 non-prosecution agreement. Ken Starr, a Kirkland partner and former Independent Counsel and Solicitor General, directly lobbied Deputy Attorney General Mark Filip in a June 19, 2008 letter [Finding #3090][EFTA00013989]. Documented later contacts between Starr and Epstein span at least eleven years after the NPA and include a March 3, 2010 conference call with Harvard economist Henry Rosovsky, a March 19, 2010 Cambridge lunch with Rosovsky and Starr, book exchanges and a lunch at Epstein's Palm Beach residence in November 2017, and further contacts through September 2018 [Finding #3078][EFTA02668810].

On November 27, 2016, Starr forwarded information to Epstein about the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), and Epstein responded, "got it, thanks. leave it in my hands. always a treat" [Finding #3078][EFTA02668810]. On June 13, 2018, Starr coordinated messaging with journalist Michael Wolff through Epstein, writing, "I gave Michael the all clear. We're going to continue to chat" [Finding #3078]. Separately, Kirkland assistant Kristin Andersen functioned as a contact point for media inquiries about Epstein; in March 2011, she forwarded journalist Alexandra Wolfe's Newsweek interview request to Lefkowitz, who coordinated a response with the PR firm Sitrick and Company [Finding #3073][EFTA02536913].

Jay Lefkowitz's family also maintained social ties with Epstein after his 2008 conviction and sex-offender registration. In February and March 2011, Elena Lefkowitz invited Epstein to a HaZamir 18th Anniversary Concert at Jazz at Lincoln Center, writing, "Jay and I would like to introduce you to the work of the Zamir Choral Foundation" [Finding #3068][EFTA02536913]. Epstein referred additional client matters to Kirkland beyond his own defense. In November 2012, Epstein coached Microsoft's former Windows president Steven Sinofsky through a severance negotiation in which Kirkland partners Scott D. Price and Lefkowitz represented Sinofsky, telling him "Push on 20 do not fold" [Finding #3063][EFTA02723303]. A Sinofsky billing record covering the period ending January 31, 2013 shows Price and Lefkowitz billed 21 hours at $1,045–$1,095 per hour, totaling roughly $22,020 [Finding #3062][EFTA02679084]. In November 2013, Kirkland attorney Jonathan A. Schechter appeared on correspondence for Starwood Capital Group's BR Guest restaurant deal in a file located in Epstein's records [Finding #3064][EFTA02726364].

sections.title: The $125 Million Pro Bono Arrangement (2025)
sections.content:
According to contemporaneous news reporting, on April 11, 2025 Kirkland & Ellis agreed to provide $125 million in pro bono legal services for causes approved by the Trump administration [Finding #3099][Finding #3158]. According to the same reporting, Chairman Jon Ballis led the negotiations on the firm's behalf [Finding #3099][Finding #3162]. Records indicate the arrangement was part of a broader $600 million commitment across five firms (Kirkland, A&O Shearman, Simpson Thacher, Latham & Watkins, and Cadwalader) that later reached approximately $1 billion across nine firms [Finding #3099][Finding #3158]. According to the reporting, terms directed pro bono work toward veterans, military, law-enforcement, and antisemitism-related causes, required a disavowal of "illegal DEI" practices, included a merit-based hiring pledge, and committed the firm to accept clients regardless of political views [Finding #3099][Finding #3158].

Records show that in exchange the EEOC withdrew letters questioning the firms' diversity, equity, and inclusion hiring practices, and the firms avoided being targeted by a threatened executive order [Finding #3099][Finding #3158]. According to Congressional correspondence, Senators Blumenthal and Schiff and Representative Raskin sent a letter to Ballis questioning whether the arrangement violated federal bribery (18 USC 201), extortion (18 USC 1951), honest-services fraud (18 USC 1346), or racketeering statutes (18 USC 1962), and requested details of Kirkland's Commerce Department work [Finding #3162]. Records indicate Kirkland associates resigned in the period that followed, and the firm withheld its 2025 partner list [Finding #3162].

According to Senate confirmation records, the $125 million commitment was concurrent with Kirkland alumni holding senior DOJ and White House posts in the second Trump administration, including John Eisenberg as AAG for the National Security Division (confirmed June 2025, 52–43 vote) and Steven Bradbury as Deputy Secretary of Transportation (confirmed March 2025, 51–46 vote) [Finding #3111][Finding #3160]. Analysis indicates a recurring pattern across the firm's alumni-and-DPA history — the 2008 Filip Memo, 2012–2017 BP and Volkswagen matters, 2018–2021 Boeing with simultaneous alumni placements, and the 2025 pro-bono agreement — in which the firm made a direct financial commitment while former partners held prosecutorial or regulatory authority over matters that can involve the firm's corporate clients [Finding #3161][Finding #3180].
